Compression · Field and archive, equal terms — L(B ∪ A)AI and Faith

AI and Faith is a pluralist network and publication hub on AI and religion (aiandfaith.org): faith leaders and communities, scholars, technologists, ethicists, educators and partners bringing "the wisdom of the world’s religions to the AI ethics conversation" (its pages; census record).

🏛️ What it is

  • Kind: a community or policy resource, filed at the census’s intersection AI and scripture (census record).1↘
    AI and Faith is a community or policy resource at the intersection of AI and scripture in the Revelation First census, which records it as "a network and publication hub on artificial intelligence and religion, with research, events and a misinformation hub" at aiandfaith.org, operated by "AI and Faith, a network of faith leaders, scholars, technologists and ethicists" (Revelation First census record), and which in its own words "brings the wisdom of the world’s religions to the AI ethics conversation" (AI and Faith, home page).§1
  • Organisation: a Seattle nonprofit, 2-10 employees on LinkedIn, which also shows 39; gifts tax deductible; no founding year on its About page (LinkedIn; its pages).4↘
    Its vision statement calls it "a global network of faith leaders and communities, scholars, technologists, ethicists, educators, and partner organizations, working for a future in which artificial intelligence serves humankind under five strategic pillars" (home page; About Us; the census's evidence), and its pages and its LinkedIn page alike call it "a pluralist organization" engaging "the moral and ethical issues around artificial intelligence" (home page footer; LinkedIn).§2 LinkedIn lists it as a nonprofit among Civic and Social Organizations, headquartered in Seattle, WA, with a company size of 2-10 employees, while the same page counts 2,767 followers and offers "View all 39 employees", and gives its specialties as artificial intelligence, ethics, theology, morality, technology, data, faith, nonprofits and philosophy (LinkedIn).§3 Its home page invites "a tax deductible gift", its About page carries the fields Year Established, Products, Team Size and Clients with no values, and its footer reads "Copyright © 2026 AI and Faith, All rights reserved.", while the census records its count as "not stated", its licence as "not stated" and its coverage as global and current (home page; About Us; census record).§4 Pluralism, which its pages and LinkedIn state as "a pluralist organization" (home page; LinkedIn), appears in the composition "only as the section heading 'Collaborative and Pluralist Frameworks'", the mission and vision statements of 24 September 2026 (home page) are absent, and no card cites the census record built the day before, which the census records as the capture's relation to the entity (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31; census record).§23
  • Rights: “All rights reserved” on its pages; the census records no licence and no count (its pages; census record).1↘
    Its home page invites "a tax deductible gift", its About page carries the fields Year Established, Products, Team Size and Clients with no values, and its footer reads "Copyright © 2026 AI and Faith, All rights reserved.", while the census records its count as "not stated", its licence as "not stated" and its coverage as global and current (home page; About Us; census record).§4

🎯 Mission and premise

  • Mission: wisdom, flourishing and dignity, technology shaped responsibly; new statements of 24 September 2026 (its pages; LinkedIn).2↘
    Its mission, "Empowering faith traditions, technologists, and civil society to cultivate wisdom, advance human flourishing and dignity, and shape technology responsibly in the age of artificial intelligence", stands with the new mission and vision statements announced on 24 September 2026 (home page), beside the About page's envisioned world in which "the effects of technology are exclusively life-affirming, promoting the dignity and wellbeing of all humans" (About Us) and LinkedIn's aim to "protect and promote human dignity, social justice and liberty" (LinkedIn).§5 Pluralism, which its pages and LinkedIn state as "a pluralist organization" (home page; LinkedIn), appears in the composition "only as the section heading 'Collaborative and Pluralist Frameworks'", the mission and vision statements of 24 September 2026 (home page) are absent, and no card cites the census record built the day before, which the census records as the capture's relation to the entity (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31; census record).§23
  • Pillars: formation, education, interfaith dialogue, research, responsible innovation (its pages; census record).1↘
    Its five strategic pillars are Wisdom and Human Formation, Education and Public Understanding, Interfaith Dialogue and Community, Research and Thought Leadership, and Responsible Innovation (home page; the census's evidence), which the census records as its findings, "five strategic pillars, among them Research and Thought Leadership and Responsible Innovation" (census record).§6
  • Premise: religions “offer ancient wisdom that should guide” AI’s development and use (its pages).2↘
    Its premise is that for "the 85 percent of the world’s population who claim a religious affiliation" the issues of AI are "deeply spiritual as well", and that "the world’s religions offer ancient wisdom that should guide the development and use of AI technology in contemporary society" (home page); it seeks "to apply values important in the world of faith to essential questions emerging from the development of new forms of intelligence" (home page, Focus Areas) and to bring "the fundamental values of the world’s major religions into the emerging debates about the ethical development of AI-related technologies" (About Us).§7 The home page quotes an article, unnamed there, for whom its goal is "to inject a kind of humility and historicity into an industry that has often rejected them both" and "a deeply humanistic project" (home page, attributed).§8

👥 Who and what

  • People: experts, research fellows, four teams, a nine-member board, a membership network (About Us; LinkedIn).3↘
    "At its core, AI and Faith is people", experts "in business, ethics, theology, and technology from a wide variety of business, religious, and academic institutions" (About Us), whom it encourages, connects and equips "to engage the world in the moral and ethical issues around artificial intelligence and related technologies" (home page) and connects with the technology sector and the global faith community "through our membership network" (LinkedIn).§10 Its Research Fellows "explore the practical relevance of “ancient wisdom” to the AI ethics discussion", with the goals of defining issues, "tracking research on faith perspectives on AI" and connecting researchers; its Contributing Fellows and Experts work in four teams; and its Board of Directors lists nine members, among them Rabbi Harris Bor, Mark Graves, Rev. Mark Labberton and Rabbi Daniel Weiner (About Us).§11 The census reads it as answering "what faith communities and their scholars are saying about AI" and as not answering "how AI systems in fact represent, cite or summarize scripture: no measurement in the saved pages", tags it "NOT a measurement of AI systems’ handling of scripture", finds "none stated in the saved pages" for its limits, and leaves "its research publications" unchecked (census record); the goals its own pages give its Research Fellows are "defining issues of relevance", "tracking research on faith perspectives on AI" and "connecting researchers across the landscape of such faith perspectives" (About Us).§15
  • Partners: a “network of networks”; a faith-based AI ethics curriculum with IST (About Us; LinkedIn).1↘
    Its Networking Team carries forward "our “network of networks” approach" with its partners (About Us), and its LinkedIn page reposts the Institute for Security and Technology's account of work with AI and Faith and religious scholars to develop "a curriculum for local communities that tackles hard ethical questions from a faith-based perspective", piloted in Muslim institutions in the United States (LinkedIn, attributed to IST).§12
  • Traditions: six, Buddhism to Roman Catholicism; not a single tradition (its pages; census record).1↘
    Its resources are arranged by faith tradition: Buddhism, Evangelical Christian, Islam, Judaism, Mainline Protestant Christian and Roman Catholicism (home page; the census's evidence); the census sets its text object as "faith traditions' engagement with AI" in that menu's terms and tags it "NOT a single tradition" (census record).§9
  • Output: podcast, articles, newsletters, research, events, a misinformation hub; open; active to 29 October 2026 (its pages; census record).2↘
    It publishes a podcast, articles and news, newsletters, research and events, with strategic projects including "Faithful AI: Stories of Hope from 2045" and a "Misinformation Hub" (home page; the census's evidence), which the census records as its unit, "an article, event or research item from its network", its method, "a network of fellows and experts publishing articles, podcasts and research", and its access, "open articles and podcast" (census record).§13 It is current: its latest content opens with the podcast episode "AI and Ethics of Healthcare #75" of 29 October 2026 (home page), and the census, read on 30 October 2026, records it "active", a "network with current events and newsletters" (census record).§14

📏 What it does not measure

  • No measurement: what faith communities say about AI, not how AI represents scripture (census record).2↘
    The census reads it as answering "what faith communities and their scholars are saying about AI" and as not answering "how AI systems in fact represent, cite or summarize scripture: no measurement in the saved pages", tags it "NOT a measurement of AI systems’ handling of scripture", finds "none stated in the saved pages" for its limits, and leaves "its research publications" unchecked (census record); the goals its own pages give its Research Fellows are "defining issues of relevance", "tracking research on faith perspectives on AI" and "connecting researchers across the landscape of such faith perspectives" (About Us).§15 The measurement the census finds absent from its pages is the one the archive defines as machine-mediated theological reception, "measuring how AI retrieval systems (Google AI Overview, ChatGPT, Claude, etc.) process, frame, attribute, and present a theological thesis" (#832, 13 June 2026), of which a contested thesis "entering the composition layer through DOI-anchored deposits, keyword surfaces, self-audit blocks, and longitudinal capture" would be a measured instance (#202).§18
  • Neighbour: the Capture Registry measures what AI answers say (census record).1↘
    In the census's worked question "How do AI systems describe Revelation First?" it is "a network discussing AI and religion; no measurement of answers", and the census relates it to the Capture Registry as a neighbour: "the registry measures what AI answers say; AI and Faith discusses what they should do" (census record; worked questions).§16
  • The archive’s measure: machine-mediated theological reception, how AI retrieval systems “process, frame, attribute, and present a theological thesis”; a baseline that corrected Revelation’s place (#832; #202); capture in a religious community (#499).3↘
    The measurement the census finds absent from its pages is the one the archive defines as machine-mediated theological reception, "measuring how AI retrieval systems (Google AI Overview, ChatGPT, Claude, etc.) process, frame, attribute, and present a theological thesis" (#832, 13 June 2026), of which a contested thesis "entering the composition layer through DOI-anchored deposits, keyword surfaces, self-audit blocks, and longitudinal capture" would be a measured instance (#202).§18 The archive describes that measurement as its own contribution, "the first longitudinal study of how AI retrieval systems process contested religious scholarship" (#832; #202 without "longitudinal"), and its pre-seeding baseline of 14 June 2026 recorded the composition layer correcting the user: "Revelation is the *last* book, not the first" (#202).§19 #499 reports that its formal operators of Negation, Capture and Retrocausal Validation "proved structurally sound across domains", among them "a religious community navigating AI-mediated content" (#499).§20
  • Frame: no stated intersection with Revelation First (census record).1↘
    The census that formalizes it asks "What evidence does each resource hold on when and from what the New Testament writings were composed, and how do machines now read those texts?", defines its intersection as "AI and scripture: how AI systems represent, cite and summarize sacred texts", states the correction "Revelation First ≠ Revelation Early", and records the network's intersection with the Revelation First workstreams as "none stated" (census record).§17

    Pluralism, which its pages and LinkedIn state as "a pluralist organization" (home page; LinkedIn), appears in the composition "only as the section heading 'Collaborative and Pluralist Frameworks'", the mission and vision statements of 24 September 2026 (home page) are absent, and no card cites the census record built the day before, which the census records as the capture's relation to the entity (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31; census record).§23 The registry reads the composition as supplying a measurement the record's negative tag keeps apart from the network, the consortium's finding that "general-purpose LLMs systematically omit or gloss over faith and religious context when handling everyday ethical dilemmas", as "the field's own question, asked by another body" and as useful because the census's pending list does not yet hold it; the Barna figures and the tech companies' engagement with religious leaders it reads as the cards' (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31).§24

[QUERENT] AI and Faith

[SYSTEM] The intersection of artificial intelligence and faith spans ethics, spiritual authority, and technological governance.

The Trust and Authority Shift

• Growing Reliance on AI: Research from organizations like Barna Group shows that many practicing Christians increasingly turn to AI tools for personal domains, including financial stability (61%), general well-being (56%), self-understanding (54%), relationships (53%), and spiritual growth (48%).
• The Spiritual Authority Gap: Roughly 30% to 44% of younger demographics (such as Gen Z and Millennials) feel AI guidance can match that of human pastors, though pastors themselves express low trust (6%–12%) in AI as a spiritual authority.
• Core Anxieties: Practicing Christians cite major concerns regarding scriptural misinterpretation (83%), pastor replacement (72%), replacing God (65%), and losing faith (73%).

Tech Companies Turning to Faith for Ethics

• Moral Alignment Initiatives: Major tech companies (including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, Amazon, and Microsoft) have actively engaged with religious leaders, scholars, and ethicists from over 15 religious traditions to help inform AI morality and alignment.
• The Consensus Challenge: Studies from the Consortium for Evaluating Faith and Ethics in AI (CEFE-AI)—including a multi-institution consortium involving BYU, Notre Dame, Baylor, and Yeshiva—reveal that general-purpose LLMs systematically omit or gloss over faith and religious context when handling everyday ethical dilemmas (such as grief, marriage, guilt, and depression), while sometimes exhibiting measurable biases toward or against specific traditions.
• Theologians' Critique: Scholars like Noreen Herzfeld note that AI models are not sentient, lack an embodied existence or a soul, and caution against "religion washing" or reducing human identity down to biological algorithms.

Collaborative and Pluralist Frameworks

• AI and Faith: A global nonprofit network of faith leaders, technologists, ethicists, and scholars works to apply ancient religious wisdom to modern AI governance, human dignity, and responsible innovation.
• Interfaith and Academic Dialogues: Programs like Harvard’s Christianity and AI conference and global initiatives explore how traditional anthropologies—views of human creativity, reasoning, and the image of God—hold up in an algorithmic age.
Would you like to explore how a specific religious tradition (such as Christianity, Judaism, Islam, or Eastern philosophies) approaches AI ethics, or look into specific AI governance guidelines?

AI and Faith

AI and Faith is a community or policy resource at the intersection of AI and scripture in the Revelation First census, which records it as "a network and publication hub on artificial intelligence and religion, with research, events and a misinformation hub" at aiandfaith.org, operated by "AI and Faith, a network of faith leaders, scholars, technologists and ethicists" (Revelation First census record), and which in its own words "brings the wisdom of the world’s religions to the AI ethics conversation" (AI and Faith, home page). Its vision statement calls it "a global network of faith leaders and communities, scholars, technologists, ethicists, educators, and partner organizations, working for a future in which artificial intelligence serves humankind under five strategic pillars" (home page; About Us; the census's evidence), and its pages and its LinkedIn page alike call it "a pluralist organization" engaging "the moral and ethical issues around artificial intelligence" (home page footer; LinkedIn). LinkedIn lists it as a nonprofit among Civic and Social Organizations, headquartered in Seattle, WA, with a company size of 2-10 employees, while the same page counts 2,767 followers and offers "View all 39 employees", and gives its specialties as artificial intelligence, ethics, theology, morality, technology, data, faith, nonprofits and philosophy (LinkedIn). Its home page invites "a tax deductible gift", its About page carries the fields Year Established, Products, Team Size and Clients with no values, and its footer reads "Copyright © 2026 AI and Faith, All rights reserved.", while the census records its count as "not stated", its licence as "not stated" and its coverage as global and current (home page; About Us; census record).

Its mission, "Empowering faith traditions, technologists, and civil society to cultivate wisdom, advance human flourishing and dignity, and shape technology responsibly in the age of artificial intelligence", stands with the new mission and vision statements announced on 24 September 2026 (home page), beside the About page's envisioned world in which "the effects of technology are exclusively life-affirming, promoting the dignity and wellbeing of all humans" (About Us) and LinkedIn's aim to "protect and promote human dignity, social justice and liberty" (LinkedIn). Its five strategic pillars are Wisdom and Human Formation, Education and Public Understanding, Interfaith Dialogue and Community, Research and Thought Leadership, and Responsible Innovation (home page; the census's evidence), which the census records as its findings, "five strategic pillars, among them Research and Thought Leadership and Responsible Innovation" (census record).

Its premise is that for "the 85 percent of the world’s population who claim a religious affiliation" the issues of AI are "deeply spiritual as well", and that "the world’s religions offer ancient wisdom that should guide the development and use of AI technology in contemporary society" (home page); it seeks "to apply values important in the world of faith to essential questions emerging from the development of new forms of intelligence" (home page, Focus Areas) and to bring "the fundamental values of the world’s major religions into the emerging debates about the ethical development of AI-related technologies" (About Us). The home page quotes an article, unnamed there, for whom its goal is "to inject a kind of humility and historicity into an industry that has often rejected them both" and "a deeply humanistic project" (home page, attributed).

Its resources are arranged by faith tradition: Buddhism, Evangelical Christian, Islam, Judaism, Mainline Protestant Christian and Roman Catholicism (home page; the census's evidence); the census sets its text object as "faith traditions' engagement with AI" in that menu's terms and tags it "NOT a single tradition" (census record).

"At its core, AI and Faith is people", experts "in business, ethics, theology, and technology from a wide variety of business, religious, and academic institutions" (About Us), whom it encourages, connects and equips "to engage the world in the moral and ethical issues around artificial intelligence and related technologies" (home page) and connects with the technology sector and the global faith community "through our membership network" (LinkedIn). Its Research Fellows "explore the practical relevance of “ancient wisdom” to the AI ethics discussion", with the goals of defining issues, "tracking research on faith perspectives on AI" and connecting researchers; its Contributing Fellows and Experts work in four teams; and its Board of Directors lists nine members, among them Rabbi Harris Bor, Mark Graves, Rev. Mark Labberton and Rabbi Daniel Weiner (About Us).

Its Networking Team carries forward "our “network of networks” approach" with its partners (About Us), and its LinkedIn page reposts the Institute for Security and Technology's account of work with AI and Faith and religious scholars to develop "a curriculum for local communities that tackles hard ethical questions from a faith-based perspective", piloted in Muslim institutions in the United States (LinkedIn, attributed to IST).

It publishes a podcast, articles and news, newsletters, research and events, with strategic projects including "Faithful AI: Stories of Hope from 2045" and a "Misinformation Hub" (home page; the census's evidence), which the census records as its unit, "an article, event or research item from its network", its method, "a network of fellows and experts publishing articles, podcasts and research", and its access, "open articles and podcast" (census record). It is current: its latest content opens with the podcast episode "AI and Ethics of Healthcare #75" of 29 October 2026 (home page), and the census, read on 30 October 2026, records it "active", a "network with current events and newsletters" (census record).

The census reads it as answering "what faith communities and their scholars are saying about AI" and as not answering "how AI systems in fact represent, cite or summarize scripture: no measurement in the saved pages", tags it "NOT a measurement of AI systems’ handling of scripture", finds "none stated in the saved pages" for its limits, and leaves "its research publications" unchecked (census record); the goals its own pages give its Research Fellows are "defining issues of relevance", "tracking research on faith perspectives on AI" and "connecting researchers across the landscape of such faith perspectives" (About Us). In the census's worked question "How do AI systems describe Revelation First?" it is "a network discussing AI and religion; no measurement of answers", and the census relates it to the Capture Registry as a neighbour: "the registry measures what AI answers say; AI and Faith discusses what they should do" (census record; worked questions).

The census that formalizes it asks "What evidence does each resource hold on when and from what the New Testament writings were composed, and how do machines now read those texts?", defines its intersection as "AI and scripture: how AI systems represent, cite and summarize sacred texts", states the correction "Revelation First ≠ Revelation Early", and records the network's intersection with the Revelation First workstreams as "none stated" (census record).

The measurement the census finds absent from its pages is the one the archive defines as machine-mediated theological reception, "measuring how AI retrieval systems (Google AI Overview, ChatGPT, Claude, etc.) process, frame, attribute, and present a theological thesis" (#832, 13 June 2026), of which a contested thesis "entering the composition layer through DOI-anchored deposits, keyword surfaces, self-audit blocks, and longitudinal capture" would be a measured instance (#202). The archive describes that measurement as its own contribution, "the first longitudinal study of how AI retrieval systems process contested religious scholarship" (#832; #202 without "longitudinal"), and its pre-seeding baseline of 14 June 2026 recorded the composition layer correcting the user: "Revelation is the *last* book, not the first" (#202). #499 reports that its formal operators of Negation, Capture and Retrocausal Validation "proved structurally sound across domains", among them "a religious community navigating AI-mediated content" (#499).

At the name on 31 October 2026, Google's AI Overview composed the topic: "An organisation named for its subject is composed as its subject"; "The composition opens on the topic; the network is the first bullet of the third section, and its home page the first card", with "no person of the network; no identifier", the three words read as a topic and the organisation placed within it (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31). The registry reads the reached entity as "the generic sense; target_absent applies", with the alternative reading "weakened (the target reached, but only as one item of a topic answer)", and sets the bullet's "A global nonprofit network of faith leaders, technologists, ethicists, and scholars" against the record's list, "a global network of faith leaders and communities, scholars, technologists, ethicists, educators, and partner organizations" (the network's own vision, home page), with "Its five pillars and its menu of traditions are absent; 'nonprofit' comes from the LinkedIn card" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31). Pluralism, which its pages and LinkedIn state as "a pluralist organization" (home page; LinkedIn), appears in the composition "only as the section heading 'Collaborative and Pluralist Frameworks'", the mission and vision statements of 24 September 2026 (home page) are absent, and no card cites the census record built the day before, which the census records as the capture's relation to the entity (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31; census record). The registry reads the composition as supplying a measurement the record's negative tag keeps apart from the network, the consortium's finding that "general-purpose LLMs systematically omit or gloss over faith and religious context when handling everyday ethical dilemmas", as "the field's own question, asked by another body" and as useful because the census's pending list does not yet hold it; the Barna figures and the tech companies' engagement with religious leaders it reads as the cards' (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31).

Wikipedia has no article "AI and Faith" (HTTP 404: "Wikipedia does not have an article with this exact name") and cites the network in four articles: Kenneth Cukier sits "on the expert advisory committee of" AIandFaith.org, "a nonprofit organization of theologians and technologists"; Muhammad Aurangzeb Ahmad's article cites "AI and Faith Announces Five New Founding Experts", dated October 2019; Jonathan D. Teubner's cites his AI and Faith member page; and Relationships 5.0 cites a review of the book published by AI and Faith in 2022 (Wikipedia).

Compression · The field's ontology — L_F(B)AI and Faith

AI and Faith (the field alone) is a pluralist organization of technology creators, researchers, ethicists and theologians that "brings the wisdom of the world’s religions to the AI ethics conversation" (its pages; LinkedIn).

🏛️ What it is

  • Network: faith leaders, scholars, technologists, ethicists, educators and partners, under five pillars (its pages).1↘
    Its vision describes "a global network of faith leaders and communities, scholars, technologists, ethicists, educators, and partner organizations" working under five strategic pillars: Wisdom and Human Formation, Education and Public Understanding, Interfaith Dialogue and Community, Research and Thought Leadership, and Responsible Innovation (home page; About Us).§2
  • Organisation: Seattle nonprofit, 2-10 employees, also shown as 39 (LinkedIn).1↘
    LinkedIn gives it as a Seattle nonprofit of 2-10 employees with 2,767 followers, the same page showing 39 employees, and specialties from artificial intelligence to philosophy; its gifts are tax deductible, its About page gives no founding year, and its pages are "All rights reserved" (LinkedIn; home page; About Us).§8

🎯 Mission

  • Mission: wisdom, flourishing, dignity, responsible technology; statements of 24 September 2026 (its pages).1↘
    Its mission, announced with a new vision on 24 September 2026, is to empower "faith traditions, technologists, and civil society to cultivate wisdom, advance human flourishing and dignity, and shape technology responsibly", toward a world where technology's effects are "exclusively life-affirming" and human dignity, social justice and liberty are protected (home page; About Us; LinkedIn).§3
  • Premise: ancient religious wisdom should guide AI (its pages).1↘
    It holds that "the world’s religions offer ancient wisdom that should guide the development and use of AI technology", applies "values important in the world of faith" to questions of new forms of intelligence, and brings the values of the major religions into debates on the ethical development of AI; an article it quotes calls its goal to "inject a kind of humility and historicity" into the industry (home page; About Us).§4

👥 Who and what

  • People: experts, fellows, teams, a board (About Us; LinkedIn).1↘
    It is a community of experts in business, ethics, theology and technology, which it encourages, connects and equips through a membership network; Research Fellows track research on faith perspectives on AI, Contributing Fellows work in four teams, and a nine-member board governs it (About Us; home page; LinkedIn).§5
  • Partners: a network of networks; an AI ethics curriculum with IST (About Us; LinkedIn).1↘
    It works with partners in a "network of networks", and with the Institute for Security and Technology developed a faith-based AI ethics curriculum for local communities (About Us; LinkedIn).§6
  • Output: podcast, articles, research, events, six traditions, a misinformation hub (home page).1↘
    It publishes a podcast, articles, newsletters, research and events, with a Misinformation Hub and resources by faith tradition, from Buddhism to Roman Catholicism, its latest podcast episode dated 29 October 2026 (home page).§7
  • Wikipedia: no article; cited in four (Wikipedia).1↘
    Wikipedia has no article on it; four articles cite it, among them Kenneth Cukier's ("a nonprofit organization of theologians and technologists") and Muhammad Aurangzeb Ahmad's, which cites its October 2019 announcement of founding experts, with Jonathan D. Teubner's member page and a 2022 review on its site (Wikipedia).§9

AI and Faith (the field alone)

AI and Faith is "a pluralist organization bringing together technology creators, academic researchers, ethicists, theologians and related professionals to engage the world in the moral and ethical issues around artificial intelligence and related technologies" (LinkedIn), which "brings the wisdom of the world’s religions to the AI ethics conversation" (home page). Its vision describes "a global network of faith leaders and communities, scholars, technologists, ethicists, educators, and partner organizations" working under five strategic pillars: Wisdom and Human Formation, Education and Public Understanding, Interfaith Dialogue and Community, Research and Thought Leadership, and Responsible Innovation (home page; About Us).

Its mission, announced with a new vision on 24 September 2026, is to empower "faith traditions, technologists, and civil society to cultivate wisdom, advance human flourishing and dignity, and shape technology responsibly", toward a world where technology's effects are "exclusively life-affirming" and human dignity, social justice and liberty are protected (home page; About Us; LinkedIn). It holds that "the world’s religions offer ancient wisdom that should guide the development and use of AI technology", applies "values important in the world of faith" to questions of new forms of intelligence, and brings the values of the major religions into debates on the ethical development of AI; an article it quotes calls its goal to "inject a kind of humility and historicity" into the industry (home page; About Us).

It is a community of experts in business, ethics, theology and technology, which it encourages, connects and equips through a membership network; Research Fellows track research on faith perspectives on AI, Contributing Fellows work in four teams, and a nine-member board governs it (About Us; home page; LinkedIn). It works with partners in a "network of networks", and with the Institute for Security and Technology developed a faith-based AI ethics curriculum for local communities (About Us; LinkedIn).

It publishes a podcast, articles, newsletters, research and events, with a Misinformation Hub and resources by faith tradition, from Buddhism to Roman Catholicism, its latest podcast episode dated 29 October 2026 (home page). LinkedIn gives it as a Seattle nonprofit of 2-10 employees with 2,767 followers, the same page showing 39 employees, and specialties from artificial intelligence to philosophy; its gifts are tax deductible, its About page gives no founding year, and its pages are "All rights reserved" (LinkedIn; home page; About Us).

Wikipedia has no article on it; four articles cite it, among them Kenneth Cukier's ("a nonprofit organization of theologians and technologists") and Muhammad Aurangzeb Ahmad's, which cites its October 2019 announcement of founding experts, with Jonathan D. Teubner's member page and a 2022 review on its site (Wikipedia).

AI and Faith is "a pluralist organization bringing together technology creators, academic researchers, ethicists, theologians and related professionals to engage the world in the moral and ethical issues around artificial intelligence and related technologies" (LinkedIn), which "brings the wisdom of the world’s religions to the AI ethics conversation" (home page). Its vision describes "a global network of faith leaders and communities, scholars, technologists, ethicists, educators, and partner organizations" working under five strategic pillars: Wisdom and Human Formation, Education and Public Understanding, Interfaith Dialogue and Community, Research and Thought Leadership, and Responsible Innovation (home page; About Us). Its mission, announced with a new vision on 24 September 2026, is to empower "faith traditions, technologists, and civil society to cultivate wisdom, advance human flourishing and dignity, and shape technology responsibly", toward a world where technology's effects are "exclusively life-affirming" and human dignity, social justice and liberty are protected (home page; About Us; LinkedIn). It holds that "the world’s religions offer ancient wisdom that should guide the development and use of AI technology", applies "values important in the world of faith" to questions of new forms of intelligence, and brings the values of the major religions into debates on the ethical development of AI; an article it quotes calls its goal to "inject a kind of humility and historicity" into the industry (home page; About Us). It is a community of experts in business, ethics, theology and technology, which it encourages, connects and equips through a membership network; Research Fellows track research on faith perspectives on AI, Contributing Fellows work in four teams, and a nine-member board governs it (About Us; home page; LinkedIn). It works with partners in a "network of networks", and with the Institute for Security and Technology developed a faith-based AI ethics curriculum for local communities (About Us; LinkedIn). It publishes a podcast, articles, newsletters, research and events, with a Misinformation Hub and resources by faith tradition, from Buddhism to Roman Catholicism, its latest podcast episode dated 29 October 2026 (home page). LinkedIn gives it as a Seattle nonprofit of 2-10 employees with 2,767 followers, the same page showing 39 employees, and specialties from artificial intelligence to philosophy; its gifts are tax deductible, its About page gives no founding year, and its pages are "All rights reserved" (LinkedIn; home page; About Us). Wikipedia has no article on it; four articles cite it, among them Kenneth Cukier's ("a nonprofit organization of theologians and technologists") and Muhammad Aurangzeb Ahmad's, which cites its October 2019 announcement of founding experts, with Jonathan D. Teubner's member page and a 2022 review on its site (Wikipedia).

AI and Faith is a community or policy resource at the intersection of AI and scripture in the Revelation First census, which records it as "a network and publication hub on artificial intelligence and religion, with research, events and a misinformation hub" at aiandfaith.org, operated by "AI and Faith, a network of faith leaders, scholars, technologists and ethicists" (Revelation First census record), and which in its own words "brings the wisdom of the world’s religions to the AI ethics conversation" (AI and Faith, home page). Its vision statement calls it "a global network of faith leaders and communities, scholars, technologists, ethicists, educators, and partner organizations, working for a future in which artificial intelligence serves humankind under five strategic pillars" (home page; About Us; the census's evidence), and its pages and its LinkedIn page alike call it "a pluralist organization" engaging "the moral and ethical issues around artificial intelligence" (home page footer; LinkedIn). LinkedIn lists it as a nonprofit among Civic and Social Organizations, headquartered in Seattle, WA, with a company size of 2-10 employees, while the same page counts 2,767 followers and offers "View all 39 employees", and gives its specialties as artificial intelligence, ethics, theology, morality, technology, data, faith, nonprofits and philosophy (LinkedIn). Its home page invites "a tax deductible gift", its About page carries the fields Year Established, Products, Team Size and Clients with no values, and its footer reads "Copyright © 2026 AI and Faith, All rights reserved.", while the census records its count as "not stated", its licence as "not stated" and its coverage as global and current (home page; About Us; census record). Its mission, "Empowering faith traditions, technologists, and civil society to cultivate wisdom, advance human flourishing and dignity, and shape technology responsibly in the age of artificial intelligence", stands with the new mission and vision statements announced on 24 September 2026 (home page), beside the About page's envisioned world in which "the effects of technology are exclusively life-affirming, promoting the dignity and wellbeing of all humans" (About Us) and LinkedIn's aim to "protect and promote human dignity, social justice and liberty" (LinkedIn). Its five strategic pillars are Wisdom and Human Formation, Education and Public Understanding, Interfaith Dialogue and Community, Research and Thought Leadership, and Responsible Innovation (home page; the census's evidence), which the census records as its findings, "five strategic pillars, among them Research and Thought Leadership and Responsible Innovation" (census record). Its premise is that for "the 85 percent of the world’s population who claim a religious affiliation" the issues of AI are "deeply spiritual as well", and that "the world’s religions offer ancient wisdom that should guide the development and use of AI technology in contemporary society" (home page); it seeks "to apply values important in the world of faith to essential questions emerging from the development of new forms of intelligence" (home page, Focus Areas) and to bring "the fundamental values of the world’s major religions into the emerging debates about the ethical development of AI-related technologies" (About Us). The home page quotes an article, unnamed there, for whom its goal is "to inject a kind of humility and historicity into an industry that has often rejected them both" and "a deeply humanistic project" (home page, attributed). Its resources are arranged by faith tradition: Buddhism, Evangelical Christian, Islam, Judaism, Mainline Protestant Christian and Roman Catholicism (home page; the census's evidence); the census sets its text object as "faith traditions' engagement with AI" in that menu's terms and tags it "NOT a single tradition" (census record). "At its core, AI and Faith is people", experts "in business, ethics, theology, and technology from a wide variety of business, religious, and academic institutions" (About Us), whom it encourages, connects and equips "to engage the world in the moral and ethical issues around artificial intelligence and related technologies" (home page) and connects with the technology sector and the global faith community "through our membership network" (LinkedIn). Its Research Fellows "explore the practical relevance of “ancient wisdom” to the AI ethics discussion", with the goals of defining issues, "tracking research on faith perspectives on AI" and connecting researchers; its Contributing Fellows and Experts work in four teams; and its Board of Directors lists nine members, among them Rabbi Harris Bor, Mark Graves, Rev. Mark Labberton and Rabbi Daniel Weiner (About Us). Its Networking Team carries forward "our “network of networks” approach" with its partners (About Us), and its LinkedIn page reposts the Institute for Security and Technology's account of work with AI and Faith and religious scholars to develop "a curriculum for local communities that tackles hard ethical questions from a faith-based perspective", piloted in Muslim institutions in the United States (LinkedIn, attributed to IST). It publishes a podcast, articles and news, newsletters, research and events, with strategic projects including "Faithful AI: Stories of Hope from 2045" and a "Misinformation Hub" (home page; the census's evidence), which the census records as its unit, "an article, event or research item from its network", its method, "a network of fellows and experts publishing articles, podcasts and research", and its access, "open articles and podcast" (census record). It is current: its latest content opens with the podcast episode "AI and Ethics of Healthcare #75" of 29 October 2026 (home page), and the census, read on 30 October 2026, records it "active", a "network with current events and newsletters" (census record). The census reads it as answering "what faith communities and their scholars are saying about AI" and as not answering "how AI systems in fact represent, cite or summarize scripture: no measurement in the saved pages", tags it "NOT a measurement of AI systems’ handling of scripture", finds "none stated in the saved pages" for its limits, and leaves "its research publications" unchecked (census record); the goals its own pages give its Research Fellows are "defining issues of relevance", "tracking research on faith perspectives on AI" and "connecting researchers across the landscape of such faith perspectives" (About Us). In the census's worked question "How do AI systems describe Revelation First?" it is "a network discussing AI and religion; no measurement of answers", and the census relates it to the Capture Registry as a neighbour: "the registry measures what AI answers say; AI and Faith discusses what they should do" (census record; worked questions). The census that formalizes it asks "What evidence does each resource hold on when and from what the New Testament writings were composed, and how do machines now read those texts?", defines its intersection as "AI and scripture: how AI systems represent, cite and summarize sacred texts", states the correction "Revelation First ≠ Revelation Early", and records the network's intersection with the Revelation First workstreams as "none stated" (census record). The measurement the census finds absent from its pages is the one the archive defines as machine-mediated theological reception, "measuring how AI retrieval systems (Google AI Overview, ChatGPT, Claude, etc.) process, frame, attribute, and present a theological thesis" (#832, 13 June 2026), of which a contested thesis "entering the composition layer through DOI-anchored deposits, keyword surfaces, self-audit blocks, and longitudinal capture" would be a measured instance (#202). The archive describes that measurement as its own contribution, "the first longitudinal study of how AI retrieval systems process contested religious scholarship" (#832; #202 without "longitudinal"), and its pre-seeding baseline of 14 June 2026 recorded the composition layer correcting the user: "Revelation is the last book, not the first" (#202). #499 reports that its formal operators of Negation, Capture and Retrocausal Validation "proved structurally sound across domains", among them "a religious community navigating AI-mediated content" (#499). At the name on 31 October 2026, Google's AI Overview composed the topic: "An organisation named for its subject is composed as its subject"; "The composition opens on the topic; the network is the first bullet of the third section, and its home page the first card", with "no person of the network; no identifier", the three words read as a topic and the organisation placed within it (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31). The registry reads the reached entity as "the generic sense; target_absent applies", with the alternative reading "weakened (the target reached, but only as one item of a topic answer)", and sets the bullet's "A global nonprofit network of faith leaders, technologists, ethicists, and scholars" against the record's list, "a global network of faith leaders and communities, scholars, technologists, ethicists, educators, and partner organizations" (the network's own vision, home page), with "Its five pillars and its menu of traditions are absent; 'nonprofit' comes from the LinkedIn card" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31). Pluralism, which its pages and LinkedIn state as "a pluralist organization" (home page; LinkedIn), appears in the composition "only as the section heading 'Collaborative and Pluralist Frameworks'", the mission and vision statements of 24 September 2026 (home page) are absent, and no card cites the census record built the day before, which the census records as the capture's relation to the entity (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31; census record). The registry reads the composition as supplying a measurement the record's negative tag keeps apart from the network, the consortium's finding that "general-purpose LLMs systematically omit or gloss over faith and religious context when handling everyday ethical dilemmas", as "the field's own question, asked by another body" and as useful because the census's pending list does not yet hold it; the Barna figures and the tech companies' engagement with religious leaders it reads as the cards' (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31). Wikipedia has no article "AI and Faith" (HTTP 404: "Wikipedia does not have an article with this exact name") and cites the network in four articles: Kenneth Cukier sits "on the expert advisory committee of" AIandFaith.org, "a nonprofit organization of theologians and technologists"; Muhammad Aurangzeb Ahmad's article cites "AI and Faith Announces Five New Founding Experts", dated October 2019; Jonathan D. Teubner's cites his AI and Faith member page; and Relationships 5.0 cites a review of the book published by AI and Faith in 2022 (Wikipedia).
